\[
n = u^{2}+v^{2}\qquad (u,v\in\mathbb Z,\;u\ge 0,\;v\ge 0)

\[

\]

\[

A lattice point \((x,y)\) lies on the circle exactly when  

\[
(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=n .
\]

Thus the number of lattice points on the circle is the number of integer solutions of  

\[
u^{2}+v^{2}=n ,\qquad u,v\in \mathbb Z .
\]

Denote this number by \(r_{2}(n)\).  A classical result from the theory of sums of two squares states  

\[
r_{2}(n)=4\bigl(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\bigr),
\]

where  

* \(d_{1}(n)\) = number of positive divisors of \(n\) that are \(\equiv 1\pmod 4\);
* \(d_{3}(n)\) = number of positive divisors of \(n\) that are \(\equiv 3\pmod 4\).

Consequently a circle of radius \(\sqrt{n}\) passes through exactly \(12\) lattice points iff  

\[
4\bigl(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\bigr)=12\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)=3 .
\]

Hence we must find all \(n<500\) for which the difference between the numbers of
\(1\pmod 4\) and \(3\pmod 4\) divisors equals three.

---

### 1.  Prime‑square case  

If \(p\) is a prime with \(p\equiv1\pmod 4\) then \(p^{2}\) has exactly the three
divisors  

\[
1,\;p,\;p^{2},
\]

all of which are \(\equiv1\pmod4\).  Thus  

\[
d_{1}(p^{2})=3,\qquad d_{3}(p^{2})=0\;\Longrightarrow\;d_{1}-d_{3}=3 .
\]

The squares of the \(1\pmod4\) primes that are below \(500\) are

\[
5^{2}=25,\qquad 7^{2}=49,\qquad 11^{2}=121,\qquad 13^{2}=169,\qquad
17^{2}=289,\qquad 19^{2}=361 .
\]

All of them satisfy the required condition.  
(We will later see that \(169\) does not affect the final sum because it will be
excluded by the counting argument below.)

The divisor set of \(p^{2}q\) consists of  

\[
1,\;p,\;p^{2},\;q,\;pq,\;p^{2}q .
\]

Among them the three numbers \(1,p,p^{2}\) are \(\equiv1\pmod4\) and the three
numbers \(q,pq,p^{2}q\) are \(\equiv3\pmod4\).  Hence \(d_{1}=3,\;d_{3}=3\) and

predictable way.  For a number \(n=2^{k}m\) with \(m\) odd, the divisors that are
\(\equiv1\pmod4\) are exactly the divisors of \(m\) that are \(\equiv1\pmod4\);
the divisors that are \(\equiv3\pmod4\) are exactly the divisors of \(m\) that are
\(\equiv3\pmod4\).  Thus the factor \(2\) does not alter the value of
\(d_{1}(n)-d_{3}(n)\).

\[
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=n .

Because the centre is a lattice point, translating the coordinates by \((-a,-b)\) does not change the number of solutions; we may therefore assume the centre is the origin.  
Consequently we are looking for the number of representations of \(n\) as a sum of two squares

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=n ,\qquad (x,y)\in\mathbb Z^{2},

### 1.  How many representations does a given \(n\) have?

If  

\[
n = 2^{\alpha}\,\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)} p^{\beta_p}\,\prod_{q\equiv 3\;(4)} q^{\gamma_q},
\]

then the number of *ordered* integer solutions of \(x^{2}+y^{2}=n\) is  

\[
r_2(n)=4\!\!\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)} (\beta_p+1),
\]

provided every \(\gamma_q\) is even (otherwise there are no solutions).  
The factor \(4\) accounts for the four quadrants; the product runs only over the primes
congruent to \(1\pmod 4\).

Thus the condition “exactly 12 lattice points’’ translates into  

\[
r_2(n)=12\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
4\!\!\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}(\beta_p+1)=12,
\]

so we need  

\[
\prod_{p\equiv 1\;(4)}(\beta_p+1)=3 .
\]

The only way to obtain a product equal to \(3\) is to have exactly **one** prime
\(p\equiv1\pmod 4\) appearing to the first power (\(\beta_p=2\)) and no other such primes.
Therefore

\[
n = p^{2}\, \bigl(\text{any square of a product of }2\text{'s and primes }q\equiv3\pmod4\bigr),
\qquad p\equiv1\pmod4 .
\]

In other words, \(n\) must contain a *single* prime factor \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) raised to the power \(2\); all other odd prime factors must be \(\equiv3\pmod4\) and appear with even exponent, while any power of \(2\) is allowed.
